findings.situation: A married-filing-separately filer whose spouse was born before January 2, 1961, had no income, isn't filing a return and can't be claimed as a dependent may check the spouse's age box, but the question limits the person to 'you, or your spouse on a joint return'.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 33, Line 12d: "If your filing status is married filing separately and your spouse was born before January 2, 1961, or was blind at the end of 2025, you can check the appropriate box(es) on line 12d if your spouse had no income, isn't filing a return, and can't be claimed as a dependent on another person's return."
findings.why: The wording tells a separate filer the question does not apply to their spouse, so the spouse's yes that the age box and the standard deduction chart (the 3 and 4 box rows for married filing separately) allow is never given.

findings.situation: A person born before January 2, 1961 who died in 2025 before reaching 65 is under age 65 for Schedule R, but the truthful yes leaves them out of the under-65 count in `s3.under65s`.
findings.source_text: i1040sr p. 1, Age 65, Death of taxpayer: "However, if the taxpayer died on February 12, 2025, the taxpayer isn't considered age 65 at the time of death or at the end of 2025."
findings.why: `s3.under65s` counts only entries answered no, and the question asks only for the birth date, so this under-65 person is missed.

findings.situation: A person born before January 2, 1961 who died in 2025 before reaching 65 truthfully answers yes to "Were you born before January 2, 1961?", and that raw yes feeds `person.senior_work_ssn` (Schedule 1-A lines 36a/36b), `s3.seniors` and `sa.age65_count` with no death check.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 110, Part V: "If a taxpayer was born before January 2, 1961, but died in 2025 before reaching age 65, then the taxpayer doesn't qualify for the enhanced deduction for seniors." i1040gi p. 33, Line 12d: "If your spouse was born before January 2, 1961, but died in 2025 before reaching age 65, don't check the box".
findings.why: Only `person.age65_box` applies the died-before-65 exclusion; the other lines take the birth-date yes as given, so the decedent is allowed the $6,000 senior deduction, counted as 65 or older for Schedule R, and counted in the standard deduction box total.

findings.situation: In 2025 the person paid tuition for an academic period that begins after March 2026 (for example, a fall 2026 semester), so a truthful answer is yes.
findings.source_text: i8863 (2025) p. 2: "the credits are based on the amount of adjusted qualified education expenses paid for the student in 2025 for academic periods beginning in 2025 or beginning in the first 3 months of 2026"
findings.why: The question asks only whether expenses were "paid in 2025". It does not limit the expenses to academic periods beginning in 2025 or January–March 2026, so a yes can open the credit lines for expenses that don't qualify for 2025.

findings.situation: The filer (or spouse) is a student claimed as a dependent on a parent's return, and the parent paid the tuition, so a truthful answer is yes.
findings.source_text: i8863 (2025) p. 2: "If a student is claimed as a dependent on another person's tax return, all qualified education expenses of the student are treated as having been paid by that person. Therefore, only that person can claim an education credit for the student."
findings.why: The question asks whether "anyone" paid the expenses, so this student answers yes. But the expenses are treated as paid by the person claiming them as a dependent, and only that person can claim the credit, so this return's credit lines must stay empty.

findings.situation: A filer bought required textbooks from an outside bookstore and is unsure whether these count as "qualified education expenses".
findings.source_text: i8863 (2025) p. 2, Table 1: AOTC qualified expenses include "course materials that the student needs for a course of study whether or not the materials are bought at the educational institution"; LLC qualified expenses are "Tuition and required enrollment fees (including amounts required to be paid to the institution for course-related books...)"
findings.why: The question doesn't say which credit's definition applies. A filer whose only 2025 payments were for such materials could reasonably answer either yes or no.

findings.situation: The institution was not required to furnish a Form 1098-T (for example, the expenses were paid entirely with scholarships), but the filer cannot show that the student was enrolled or cannot substantiate payment of qualified tuition.

findings.why: The question applies "you can show the enrollment and the payments" only to the not-furnished branch. findings.situation: A student's tax-free scholarship for one academic period is more than that period's qualified expenses, and the filer reports one combined amount for the whole year, so the excess reduces another period's expenses.
findings.source_text: i8863 p. 9: "Complete a separate worksheet for each student for each academic period"; "4. ... Subtract line 3 from line 1. If zero or less, enter -0-". Question: "Tax-free educational assistance received in 2025 for this student's 2025 expenses"
findings.why: The worksheet nets assistance against expenses one academic period at a time, with a floor of zero. A single year total lets excess assistance from one period offset expenses of another, which understates adjusted qualified education expenses.

findings.situation: A student who is a sole proprietor or partner in a business where capital is a material income-producing factor counts all of their net profit as pay for personal services, so earned income looks at least half of support and they answer no, while the capped figure is less than half and the lines need yes.
findings.source_text: i8863 p. 7, Earned income: "earned income also includes a reasonable allowance for compensation for personal services, but not more than 30% of your share of the net profits from that trade or business (after subtracting the deduction for one-half of self-employment tax)"
findings.why: The question leaves out the 30% cap and the reduction for half of self-employment tax. Without them, earned income is overstated and a required yes becomes no.

findings.situation: A shareholder-employee whose corporate pay is partly a distribution of earnings counts the full amount as wages, gets earned income of at least half of support and answers no, while the lines need yes.
findings.source_text: i8863 p. 7, Earned income: "Earned income doesn't include that part of the compensation for personal services rendered to a corporation which represents a distribution of earnings or profits rather than a reasonable allowance as compensation"
findings.why: The question's definition of earned income has no exclusion for compensation that is really a distribution of profits, so a truthful filer overstates earned income.

findings.situation: A student who lives rent-free in a parent's home gives that lodging no value, or only the parent's cash cost, and finds earned income at least half of support, while support measured at fair market value makes the answer yes.
findings.source_text: i8863 p. 7, Support: "If the item of support is in the form of property or lodging, measure the amount of such item of support by its fair market value."
findings.why: The question names shelter as support but does not say to value lodging or property at fair market value, so support can be understated and a required yes missed.

findings.situation: A filer deciding whether a scholarship counts as support cannot tell what 'full-time student' means here, and may use their school's own enrollment status instead of the five-month test.
findings.source_text: i8863 p. 7, Full-time student: "Solely for purposes of determining whether a scholarship is considered support, you were a full-time student for 2025 if during any part of any 5 calendar months during the year you were enrolled as a full-time student"
findings.why: The question uses 'full-time student' without the five-month definition. A filer who was full-time for only part of the year could read it either way, which changes whether the scholarship counts as support.

findings.source_text: i8863 p. 4: "If you or the student takes a deduction for higher education expenses, such as on Schedule C (Form 1040), you cannot use those same expenses in your qualified education expenses"; "Any qualified expenses used to figure the education credits cannot be taken into account in determining the amount of a distribution from a Coverdell ESA or a qualified tuition program (section 529 plan) that is excluded from gross income." i8863 p. 4 also excludes "Personal expenses" and "Any course or other education involving sports, games, or hobbies, or any noncredit course, unless ... part of the student's degree program"

findings.situation: The person reports notary public fees as net profit on Schedule C, and none of the listed items applies, so the filer answers no.
findings.source_text: i1040sse p. 4, Income and Losses Not Included in Net Earnings From Self-Employment, item 2: "Fees received for services performed as a notary public. If you had no other income subject to SE tax, check box number 3 and enter 'Exempt—Notary' on Schedule 2 (Form 1040), line 4. Don't file Schedule SE. However, if you had other earnings ... enter 'Exempt—Notary' and the amount of your net profit as a notary public from Schedule C on the dotted line to the left of Schedule SE, line 3. Subtract that amount..."
findings.why: Schedule C notary profit must be taken out of SE earnings through a special entry, which the tool's ordinary Schedule C path cannot do. The list does not mention notary fees, so the gate stays closed and the tool includes them in SE tax.

findings.situation: The person is a statutory employee whose W-2 income and expenses are reported on Schedule C (statutory employee box), and nothing on the list applies, so the filer answers no.

findings.situation: A self-employed filer's SEP plan states a contribution rate of 8 1/2% (or 10 1/2%), but the question accepts only a whole number, so the filer cannot enter the rate that steps 4 to 6 need.

findings.situation: A participant age 50 or over in a SIMPLE IRA plan of an employer that elected the section 117 higher limits has a catch-up limit of $3,850. The three age choices cannot express this, so the line would look up $3,500.

findings.why: The question asks only for an age band, but the line uses the answer as the whole of 'Catch-up eligibility'. Nothing in the question captures the employer-dependent $3,850 limit, so these filers get too low a limit.

findings.situation: A participant who turned 61 in 2025 is in a SIMPLE plan that did not adopt the section 109 higher catch-up. They truthfully answer age60_63, and the line gives $5,250 instead of $3,500.
findings.source_text: p560 p. 16: "section 109 of the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 permits SIMPLE plans ... to allow participants to make a higher amount of catch-up contributions in a tax year in which they attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63."
findings.why: The text makes the higher limit depend on what the plan allows, not on age alone. The question asks only age, yet the label and the line treat the answer as eligibility for the $5,250 limit.

findings.situation: A participant age 50 or over is in a SIMPLE IRA plan that does not permit catch-up contributions at all. The lines need a zero catch-up limit, but the list has no choice for this.
findings.source_text: p560 p. 16: "A SIMPLE IRA plan can permit participants who are age 50 or over at the end of the calendar year to also make catch-up contributions."
findings.why: Catch-up eligibility depends on plan permission. A truthful age answer of age50 or age60_63 yields a positive limit where the text allows none.
findings.bound: catch-up limit of 0 (plan does not permit), $3,500, $3,850 (section 117 employer), or $5,250 (age 60-63, plan permits)

findings.situation: A filer who adopted their spouse's child, or adopted someone 18 or older who can support themselves, and took a distribution counts that adoption, so the line adds another $5,000 to the cap.
findings.source_text: p590b p. 28: "an eligible adoptee is any individual (other than the child of the taxpayer's spouse) who has not reached age 18 or is physically or mentally incapable of self-support."
findings.why: The question counts any adoption the filer took a distribution for. It never limits the count to an eligible adoptee, so adoptions that cannot support a qualified birth or adoption distribution are counted.

findings.situation: A filer counts a birth or adoption even though the distribution came more than one year after the birth or after the adoption became final.
findings.source_text: p590b p. 28: "any distribution from an applicable eligible retirement plan if made during the 1-year period beginning on the date on which your child was born or the date on which the legal adoption of your child was finalized."
findings.why: The wording counts any birth or adoption the filer "took the birth or adoption distributions" for. It leaves out the 1-year window, so a late distribution still raises the cap.

findings.situation: A filer counts a child born in an earlier year whose distribution was taken in that earlier year, so the cap rises even though no distribution this year relates to that child.
findings.source_text: Question: "For how many births or adoptions ... did you take the birth or adoption distributions?"; p590b p. 28: "A qualified birth or adoption distribution must not exceed $5,000 per taxpayer."
findings.why: The question gives no year. A truthful count can include births or adoptions covered by distributions in earlier years, which inflates this year's cap on line 2.

findings.situation: A filer with two births or adoptions answers 2, and the line sets a $10,000 cap.
findings.source_text: p590b p. 28: "A qualified birth or adoption distribution must not exceed $5,000 per taxpayer."
findings.why: The cited text sets a limit per taxpayer, not per child. Under this text, any count above 1 lets the line exclude more than the $5,000 the text allows.
